newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Revival of Jardine Fleming fund seen taking time.
newsitem.headline: Revival of Jardine Fleming fund seen taking time.

text.p: Jardine Fleming Holdings Ltd hopes chairman Alan Smith's resignation last week will act as a punctuation mark between old and new following a recent trading scandal that exposed serious misconduct at the firm.

But competitors warned that Jardine Fleming has a long way to go to convince clients and rivals that the problems are truly over at subsidiary Jardine Fleming Investment Management, a company renowned for its high-flying and aggressive fund management style.

"I think, personally, that if my firm had to face that problem it would take quite a long time to resolve and it would take a lot of hard work to convince your clients (that things were resolved)," said the Hong Kong-based chief investment officer at a major fund management company who did not want to be identified.

Regulators slapped Jardine Fleming with a fine of 700,000 stg and withdrew the authorisation of its London-based fund company last month following revelations of the late allocation of trades by a senior fund manager in Hong Kong.
Jardine Fleming also paid US$19.3 million in compensation to disadvantaged clients.
Smith announced his retirement on Thursday, when the company unveiled a new two-tier board structure that added a new supervisory board.

Local newspaper reports said Smith, who is attending a conference in Europe, resigned because he objected to the new corporate structure, but rival fund managers said that once the seriousness of the fund trading scandal was understood, Smith's resignation was virtually inevitable.
"Given what happened, this is not a surprise," said Gary Greenberg, deputy managing director at Peregrine Asset Management in Hong Kong.
Said another chief investment officer: "After that case being published, he could not stay on."

A Jardine Fleming spokesman on Friday stressed Jardine Fleming's desire to "draw a line" between the company's past and future, but conceded that Colin Armstrong, the senior fund manager at the centre of the scandal, held extensive influence at the firm.
"Effectively he was the chief investment officer," the spokesman said.
Another rival chief investment officer doubted that the company's culture would change overnight, given Armstrong's prominence.
"He was the top guy there. He managed a lot of funds. The transaction amounts were huge. I don't think he could do it alone," the second chief investment officer said.
Regulators repeatedly said at the time the penalties were meted out that they were convinced Jardine Fleming would act within a culture of compliance from now on.
But observers warned that the scandal could torpedo Jardine Fleming's claim as the largest fund manager in Hong Kong with US$22 billion under management.
"The chances are big they'll lose their status as number one," the second chief investment officer said. "I'm quite sure accounts will be lost. Other fund managers will have an advantage."

Jardine Fleming previously denied that an extraordinary number of redemptions were occurring, but competitors said company reports early next year would reveal clearly the state of affairs at Jardine Fleming Investment Management.
HSBC Asset Management, one of Jardine Fleming's greatest rivals with US$40 billion invested globally, said they have experienced no windfall as a consequence of the Jardines scandal.
"There's no evidence of that whatsoever," said managing director Christopher Ryan.
